newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan newspapers expect Gujral to reduce tension.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan newspapers expect Gujral to reduce tension.

text.p: Pakistani newspapers on Monday welcomed Inder Kumar Gujral's appointment as Indian prime minister, saying he would seek better ties with Pakistan.

"One of the best things about his becoming India's next prime minister is that the process of normalisation of ties between India and Pakistan will move ahead," said the English-language newspaper The News.

"In India, with the selection of I.K. Gujral as prime minister, stability is expected to return to the world's largest democracy," the paper said. "Such a development is conducive to reducing tensions in the region, and we hope mutual efforts will be made to accelerate the pace of normalisation."
The Frontier Post said Gujral, as foreign minister in the outgoing government led by H.D. Deve Gowda, had built himself an image of providing drive and focus to India's foreign policy.

"He...was largely responsible for getting the stalled Pakistan-India dialogue started," the paper said. "He has been pitching for greater regional economic integration, a philosophy backed by the United States and pragmatists in South Asia." The daily, describing Gujral as a "shrewd politician with a vision", said his views were a departure from what it called "the usual hawkish Indian hegemony in the neighbourhood as a spring-board for a global role".
It said he would seek closer economic ties with Pakistan, but it would be naive to expect him to engineer a major shift in his country's policy on the disputed Kashmir region.

Lahore-based newspaper The Nation said the resolution of India's three-week political crisis had averted the need for fresh elections, which might have ushered in a government led by the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
Now, it said, India-Pakistan talks that resumed at the end of March after a three-year break were likely to continue.
"Regardless of whether these would bear fruit eventually or not, there is at least a sense of continuity now," it added.
The Nation said Pakistan could not withdraw its support for Kashmiris in the Indian state of Jammu and Kashmir, where Moslem rebels have waged a seven-year-old revolt against Indian rule.

"To expect that Pakistan would leave most of the Kashmiri Moslems at the tender mercies of Indian troops would be great folly. To talks we say yes. But to abandoning Kashmiris we say no," the newspaper said.
